title: Part 2, Chapter 39
paragraphs: In which the Trifaldi continues her marvelous and memorable story

Every word out of Sancho's mouth delighted the duchess as much as it drove Don Quixote to despair. He ordered him to be quiet, and the Distressed One continued: “In the end, after a great deal of questioning and answering, since the princess stuck to her story and never changed or backed away from her original declaration, the Vicar ruled in Don Clavijo's favor, and she was handed over to him as his lawful wife. Queen Doña Maguncia, Princess Antonomasia's mother, took this so much to heart that within three days we had buried her.”
“She must have died, then,” said Sancho.
“Naturally,” said Trifaldin; “in Kandy they don't bury people alive, only the dead ones.”

“Señor Squire,” said Sancho, “people in a faint have been buried before now because everyone believed they were dead, and it seems to me Queen Maguncia should have settled for fainting instead of dying. While there's life, a great many things sort themselves out, and the princess's blunder wasn't so terrible that she needed to take it so hard. If the lady had married one of her pages, or some other servant of the household, as plenty of others have done, from what I hear, then the damage would have been beyond repair. But marrying a gentleman as polished and accomplished as the one just described to us—honestly, truly, even if it was a foolish thing to do, it wasn't nearly as foolish as you think. By my master's own rules here—and he won't let me tell a lie—just as men of letters are made into bishops, so gentlemen knights, especially the errant kind, can be made into kings and emperors.”

“You are right, Sancho,” said Don Quixote, “for if a knight-errant has even two fingers' width of good luck, he stands every chance of becoming the greatest lord on earth. But let señora the Distressed One go on, for I suspect she still has the bitter part of this so-far-sweet story to tell us.”

“The bitter part is indeed still to come,” said the countess, “and bitter enough to make colocynth taste sweet and oleander seem delicious by comparison. Well then, the queen being truly dead and not merely in a faint, we buried her; and we had scarcely covered her with earth, scarcely spoken our last farewells, when—_quis talia fando temperet a lachrymis?_—there appeared above the queen's grave, mounted on a wooden horse, the giant Malambruno, Maguncia's first cousin, a man who is not only cruel but an enchanter as well. To avenge his cousin's death, to punish Don Clavijo's audacity, and out of fury at Antonomasia's defiance, he used his arts to enchant them both right there on the grave: she was turned into a brass ape, and he into a hideous crocodile of some unknown metal, while between the two there stands a pillar, likewise of metal, inscribed with certain characters in the Syriac language, which, translated into Kandian and now into Castilian, read as follows: ‘These two reckless lovers shall not regain their former shapes until the valiant Manchegan comes to meet me in single combat, for the Fates have reserved this unprecedented adventure for his great valor alone.’ When this was done, he drew an enormous broad scimitar from its sheath, seized me by the hair, and made as if to slit my throat and cut my head clean off. I was paralyzed with terror, my voice froze in my throat, and I was in utter anguish; even so I gathered what strength I could and, in a trembling, pitiful voice, said such things to him that I persuaded him to hold back from carrying out so harsh a punishment. He then had all the duennas of the palace—the ones you see here—brought before him, and after dwelling on the enormity of our offense, and railing against duennas, their characters, their wicked habits and still worse schemes, blaming all of them for what I alone had done, he declared that he would not put us to death, but would inflict slower punishments on us that would amount to perpetual civil death; and the very moment he stopped speaking, we all felt the pores of our faces opening and stinging, as though pricked with needle points. We immediately put our hands to our faces and found ourselves in the condition you see now.”

At this the Distressed One and the other duennas lifted the veils that covered them and revealed faces all bristling with beards—some red, some black, some white, and some gray—a sight at which the duke and duchess made a show of astonishment. Don Quixote and Sancho were dumbfounded, and the onlookers struck speechless, while the Trifaldi continued: “This is how that malicious villain Malambruno punished us, covering the softness and delicacy of our faces with these coarse bristles! If only heaven had let him strike off our heads with that enormous scimitar of his instead of darkening the light of our faces with this wool-stubble that covers us! For consider the matter, sirs—and what I am about to say I would say with my eyes streaming like fountains, except that the thought of our misfortune, and the oceans they have already wept, keep them as dry as barley stalks, so I say it without tears—where, I ask you, can a duenna with a beard go? What father or mother will take pity on her? Who will come to her aid? If even with a smooth complexion, and a face tormented by a thousand kinds of lotions and cosmetics, she can scarcely find anyone to love her, what is she to do when she shows a face that has turned into a thicket? Oh duennas, my companions! We were born in an unlucky moment, and it was an ill-starred hour when our fathers begot us!” And with these words she seemed about to faint.
